lead: A contour is an imaginary line on the ground joining points of equal reduced level; the shoreline of a still lake is one. A map with contours drawn at equal height steps shows the third dimension on flat paper: where the lines crowd, the ground is steep; where they spread, it is gentle. Contour maps are used to choose sites, align roads and canals at a fixed gradient, mark catchments, find the area flooded behind a dam and estimate earthwork. Contouring needs levelling, so it builds directly on the booking and reduction methods.
prereq: You need: RLs from the height of collimation method in Booking and reduction of levels.

blocks.text: The contour interval (CI), also called the vertical interval, is the constant difference in RL between successive contours on a map, for example 1 m or 2 m. The horizontal equivalent (HE) is the horizontal distance between two successive contours at a place; it changes from place to place with the slope.
HE = CI ÷ tan θ = CI × n   (ground gradient 1 in n)
blocks.where: θ is the ground slope angle and n the gradient expressed as 1 vertical in n horizontal. Halving the gradient (1 in 25 instead of 1 in 50) halves the HE, so the contours come closer.

blocks.text: The CI depends on the purpose, the map scale, the steepness of the ground (steep ground needs a larger CI or the lines merge) and the time and money available: typically 0.25 m to 1 m on a 1:500 or 1:1000 site plan, and 10 m or 20 m on a 1:50 000 sheet.

items: All points on one contour have the same RL. Every contour closes on itself, within the map or beyond its edge.
Contours close together mean steep ground; widely spaced means gentle ground; equally spaced means a uniform slope; straight, parallel and equally spaced lines mean a plane surface.
Closed contours with higher values inside show a hill; with lower values inside, a depression (pond or pit).
Across a valley, contours form V or U shapes pointing uphill, because the valley floor rises upstream. Across a ridge, they form V or U shapes pointing downhill.
Two contours of different RL do not cross or meet, except at a vertical cliff (where they merge) or an overhanging cliff (where they cross, the hidden one dashed).
The direction of steepest slope, which water follows, is at right angles to the contours.

blocks.text: Direct method. Points on each contour are found in the field. From the HI, a contour of RL H needs the staff reading HI − H; the staffman moves up or down the slope until the reading matches, and the point is pegged and fixed in plan. Accurate but slow; suits small areas.

Indirect method. Spot levels are taken and contours interpolated between them. The points can be a grid of squares (block levelling, 5 m to 20 m sides), cross-sections along a route, radial lines from a station on a hill, or tacheometric points on rough ground.

blocks.where: Interpolation by calculation: a contour of RL H crosses the line from A (RL H<sub>A</sub>) to B (RL H<sub>B</sub>) at x from A, with L the plan distance AB, assuming a uniform slope. Estimation by eye and the graphical method (a tracing of parallel lines) are faster but rougher.

items: Sections and intervisibility: a line across the map gives the ground profile and shows whether two points see each other.
Route location at a fixed gradient: for a gradient of 1 in n, set dividers to HE = CI × n at map scale and step from contour to contour; the points joined form the grade contour.
Catchment: the ridge line around a valley, traced across the contours, bounds the catchment area.

Reservoir and earthwork: the area inside the contour at full supply level is the submerged area, and contour areas give capacity and cut-and-fill volumes, as worked in Areas, volumes and reservoir capacity from contours.

examples.question: A site was levelled on 20 m squares (block levelling). The RLs of the grid points are: row A (north): A1 101.6, A2 102.4, A3 103.5; row B: B1 100.8, B2 101.7, B3 102.6; row C (south): C1 100.2, C2 100.9, C3 101.8 m. Columns 1 to 3 run west to east. Interpolate the 101 m, 102 m and 103 m contours and describe the ground.
steps: No other grid line has its two ends on opposite sides of these values, so each contour crosses only the lines listed. Join the crossing points in each square in order.

Spacing: across the grid diagonal from C1 (100.2) to A3 (103.5) the ground rises 3.3 m in 56.6 m, about 1 in 17; the contours run from north-west to south-east and the ground rises towards the north-east corner.
examples.answer: 101 m crosses at 15.0 m from A1, 4.4 m from B1, 17.5 m from B2 and 2.2 m from C2; 102 m at 10.0 m from A1, 11.4 m from A2, 6.7 m from B2 and 15.0 m from B3; 103 m at 10.9 m from A2 and 11.1 m from A3. The ground is a fairly even slope rising to the north-east.

examples.question: (a) In direct contouring, the HI is 101.235 m. What staff readings locate the 100.0 m, 100.5 m and 99.5 m contours? (b) A road must climb at 1 in 25 on a 1:2500 map with a 2 m contour interval. What divider spacing is used to plot the grade contour?
steps: (b) HE on the ground = CI × n = 2 × 25 = 50 m.
On the map, 50 m ÷ 2500 = 0.020 m = 20 mm. Set the dividers to 20 mm and step from each contour to the next.
examples.answer: (a) 1.235 m, 0.735 m and 1.735 m. (b) 20 mm between successive contours.

traps: Reading close contours as high ground. Close means steep; height is read from the values.
Interpolating across a grid line whose ends are both above (or both below) the contour value. A contour crosses only a line whose ends lie on opposite sides of it.
Using CI ÷ n for the horizontal equivalent. HE = CI × n for a gradient of 1 in n (2 m × 25 = 50 m).
Forgetting the scale when plotting HE: 50 m on the ground is 20 mm at 1:2500.

quiz.q: Define contour interval and horizontal equivalent.
quiz.a: Contour interval: the constant RL difference between successive contours. Horizontal equivalent: the horizontal distance between two successive contours at a place.

quiz.q: Why do contours bend upstream where they cross a valley?
quiz.a: The valley floor rises upstream, so a contour of fixed RL has to go further upstream along the floor before it meets ground of its own height; the line bends into a V pointing uphill.

quiz.q: When is the direct method preferred to the indirect method?
quiz.a: On small, fairly open sites where high accuracy is wanted, such as a building plot or a reservoir rim; the indirect method is faster for large or rough areas.

quiz.q: Two spot levels 30 m apart have RLs 102.6 m and 105.1 m. Where does the 104 m contour cross the line, from the lower point?
On a 1:5000 map two 5 m contours are 4 mm apart. Find the ground gradient.
quiz.a: HE = 4 mm × 5000 = 20 m; gradient = 5 in 20 = 1 in 4 (25 %).

quiz.q: In the grid example, the RL of B2 is found to be 102.7 m, not 101.7 m. What changes in the contour pattern?
quiz.a: B2 rises above A2 and B3, so the 102 m contour, which passed north and east of B2, now passes west and south of it (crossing B1–B2 and B2–C2), and B2 sits on a spur running down from A3. The 101 m contour moves from 4.4 m to 2.1 m from B1. One wrong spot level changes the shape of the ground, so spot levels are checked before the contours are drawn.

beyond: Not for the exam. Contours today are generated from a digital elevation model: a surface built from total station points, GNSS, drone photogrammetry or airborne LiDAR, usually as a triangulated irregular network (TIN), and GIS software threads contours at any interval. Flood mapping, slope analysis and cut-and-fill for highways all work on the same surface. Search for TIN interpolation, DEM from LiDAR and contour generation in QGIS.

figure.caption: The grid of the worked example with its spot levels and the 101 m, 102 m and 103 m contours joined through the interpolated crossing points. The lines are evenly spaced, so the slope is fairly uniform, rising towards A3.
